https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c0qx.text: Figure caption, Video shows scale of flash flood hitting Nepal-Tibet border By Soutik Biswas ,Â India Correspondent Â and Â Phanindra Dahal ,Â BBC Nepali Published 4 hours ago The video lasts only seconds. A dark wall appears from behind the buildings at Gyirong, on the Chinese side of the Nepal-Tibet border. At first, it looks almost like a black cloud. Then it gathers shape and speed: water, mud, boulders, ice and rock surging down the valley. The timestamp on the CCTV footage reads 10:59:53 local time. What happened in the minutes that followed is still difficult to reconstruct. But fragments of video and satellite imagery from before and after the disaster have begun to reveal the scale of the destruction. Much of the border complex appears to have been swept away, with buildings that once crowded the valley floor simply gone. Gyirong was one of the places devastated by the floods that tore through the region on 26 August. Just across the frontier, at Rasuwagadhi in Nepal's Rasuwa district, the destruction was also extensive. The Friendship Bridge linking Nepal and China was swept away, along with Nepal's immigration and customs facilities. Timure, the small trading settlement clustered around the crossing, was devastated. Image source, Satellite image (c) 2026 Vantor Image caption, A satellite image shows the area around the Nepal-China border before devastating floods swept away buildings and vehicles "This is a historic travel route between Kathmandu and Tibet. The area is geologically vulnerable, characterised by deep gorges and steep rivers that flow at high velocity, carry heavy sediment and can bring down huge boulders," says Ajay Dixit, a Kathmandu-based hydrologist. The route remains an important gateway between Nepal and China. It is a place where pilgrims heading towards Mount Kailash cross paths with traders travelling between Nepal and China, truck drivers, customs officials, tourists and people who live along the border. On the morning of the flood, more than 100 Indians may have been in or around the crossing. At least 275 Indians remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry. Nepal's Department of Immigration has been trying to reconstruct who passed through Rasuwagadhi in the final hours before the disaster. Electronic records show that 89 Nepali and foreign nationals had cleared immigration to leave Nepal for Tibet, while four people had registered their entry into Nepal. Image source, SOCIAL MEDIA/via REUTERS Image caption, CCTV footage shows people fleeing as mud and water engulf buildings at the Nepal-China border in Gyirong on 26 August The immigration system recorded its final transaction at 8:35:03am local time (10:52am Tibet time), less than 10 minutes before the torrent appeared on the CCTV footage at Gyirong. Four immigration employees, including the head of the Rasuwagadhi office, went missing in the floods. His body was later recovered far downstream. The female official who recorded the final transactions is still missing. Among the foreign nationals recorded leaving Nepal that morning were 32 Indians, 12 Chinese nationals and nine Americans, as well as citizens of Britain, Canada, Australia and Italy. Tika Ram Pokharel, a senior immigration assistant at Rasuwagadhi, was the only member of his office known to have survived. He had travelled to Kathmandu to sit an exam that day. But he says the electronic records capture only part of what was happening at the border that morning. The immigration office stood at Ghatte Khola Bazar, about 1.5km north of Timure. From there, it was another 2km to the Friendship Bridge marking the border with Tibet. Along that stretch were shops, hotels and parking areas where travellers and vehicles gathered before crossing. The Nepalese immigration office opened at 08:00, Pokharel says. Once travellers had cleared immigration, they could continue towards the border or wait in the area before crossing. Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images Image caption, Flooding in Rasuwagadhi destroyed the Friendship Bridge, roads and a hydropower substation, and swept away vehicles in Rasuwa, Nepal, last July When Pokharel called a colleague at 08:20 that morning, he was told the crossing was unusually busy. Around 300 to 400 people were waiting to leave Nepal for Tibet, he says, while others arriving from the Chinese side were also in the area. "Those who completed the immigration formalities that morning, I don't think were able to complete their immigration process on the Chinese side," Pokharel told the BBC. Pokharel says it took 15 to 20 minutes to walk from the Nepalese immigration office to the bridge after travellers had cleared immigration. Travellers arriving late the previous afternoon sometimes had to wait until the border reopened the next morning, while those travelling in groups or by bus would often wait for everyone to clear immigration before moving on together. That makes it difficult to know where those 89 people were when the flood struck. At 8:37am - less than two minutes after the immigration system recorded its final transaction - seismic instruments detected movement in the mountains above the border, according to a timeline compiled by Nepal's Centre of Hydrology and Water Resources Research. Researchers later attributed the signal to the collapse of part of a glacier that triggered the flood. China said the mudslide reached the border crossing from its origin in around seven minutes. Image caption, Tika Ram Pokharel, senior immigration assistant at the Rasuwagadhi Immigration Office, was the only staff member to survive. He was in Kathmandu for an exam when the floods struck People at the crossing could have been making their way towards the bridge, waiting in Ghatte Khola or preparing to cross towards the Chinese facility. Exactly where each person was remains unclear. And Ghatte Khola itself was far more than a waiting area. Pokharel says 50 to 60 houses stood there, alongside hotels, local businesses and four hydropower offices. It was also the final stop for buses from Kathmandu, and a base for drivers, helpers, tourist guides and cargo workers waiting for customs clearance. Travellers heading into Tibet often queued there from the previous day. "My 40-50 close friends are missing," Pokharel said. Pokharel believes the toll there could be far higher than official figures suggest, estimating that "2,000 to 2,500 people" may have been caught in the flood. The figure is his estimate and has not been independently verified. Image source, Reuters Image caption, More than 100 Indians may have been at the crossing when the flood struck. At least 275 remain missing in Nepal, according to India's foreign ministry. The immigration office itself stood about 100 metres above the river, Pokharel says. But during the flood, the water appeared to surge even higher. He initially hoped his missing colleagues might have escaped to grazing land several kilometres away. For some of the Indian pilgrims at the border, the morning had begun almost casually. They made video calls and reels for relatives back home, showing them the mountains as they waited for the Chinese immigration office to open. Sudipto Bhattacharya was receiving messages from his wife, Subhrasree Chakraborty, who was travelling with a group of more than 60 people. At 07:57 Nepal time, she sent him a photograph of the departure stamp in her passport: Nepalese immigration was done. Six minutes later, at 08:03, she sent another message: "We are waiting to enter China." Then the messages stopped. Among those at the Chinese immigration facility was a group of 77 pilgrims associated with the Isha Foundation, returning from Mount Kailash. They, along with three staff members, were unaccounted for after the flood swept through the area. Image source, China News Service/VCG via Getty Images Image caption, Rescuers carry out search and rescue operations at the mudslide-hit area in Gyirong When a 21-member Chinese rescue team reached Gyirong on 28 August, one rescuer told Chinese state media: "As far as the eye could see, there was nothing but ruins." The crossing had only recently recovered from another major flood. In July 2025, flooding shut Rasuwagadhi for nearly six months. It reopened on 1 January after China built a temporary bridge. Traffic had since returned. Chinese border authorities say more than 100,000 people had passed through Gyirong by June, while Nepali immigration records show 53,742 arrivals and departures at Rasuwagadhi in the year to mid-July. The two figures are based on different reporting periods and counting systems, making a direct comparison difficult. Indians were the largest group recorded at the Nepali immigration point, followed by Nepalis and Chinese. Gyirong had also become one of the main arteries linking Nepal and China. Posh Raj Pandey, chairman emeritus of the Kathmandu-based South Asia Watch on Trade, Economics and Environment, says Rasuwagadhi is one of Nepal's two main trading points with China, alongside Tatopani, and accounts for about a third of Nepal's $2.95bn trade with its northern neighbour. Around 60 to 70 trucks passed through the gorge each day, carrying electronics, machinery, vehicles, fruit, clothing and other goods towards Kathmandu. Pandey says the route also handled about 80% of Nepal's electric-vehicle imports from China. Its closure has left Nepal increasingly dependent on Tatopani - which Chinese authorities have also temporarily closed , external because of landslide risks on the Nepali side, the Kathmandu Post reports. The crossing also lies along the proposed route of the railway connecting the region to Kathmandu, part of plans by Nepal and China to develop a trans-Himalayan rail network. "Nepal should develop an alternative China trade route and reconsider its wider development strategy, including its heavy concentration of hydropower projects along the same river system," Pandey says. "We have put all eggs here. We need to develop an alternative border port." Across the border, Pokharel was left thinking about conversations he had with the colleagues who were now missing. The previous year's flood had made staff at the Rasuwagadhi immigration office acutely aware of the danger. At night, he says, they sometimes "felt vibrations" and went outside to check the river. They had even discussed among themselves about escaping uphill if another flood struck. "But my friends could not get that chance," he said. https://www.theyeshivaworld.com/news/gen.text: SHOCK IN POLAND: Tractor Drives Over Jewish Graves, Human Remains Scattered During Cemetery Renovations August 23, 2026 3:55 pm 3 Comments A major scandal has erupted in Poland after renovation work at a historic Jewish cemetery reportedly resulted in heavy machinery driving over kevarim and matzeivos, damaging dozens of graves and scattering human remains throughout the cemetery. The incident occurred at the Jewish cemetery in Brzesko, known in Yiddish as Briegel, where a tractor was brought in as part of work to lay foundations for the reconstruction of a collapsed cemetery wall. According to J-nerations, an organization involved in preserving Jewish heritage sites across Europe, the work was carried out without appropriate halachic supervision. The tractor allegedly drove directly across kevarim and matzeivos, shattering numerous stones, while excavation work penetrated burial areas. Fragments of human bones were subsequently found scattered at the site. The renovation project was initiated by the Jewish community of Krakow, which controls the cemetery. Those familiar with the incident have leveled severe criticism at the manner in which the work was conducted and questioned how heavy excavation could have been permitted at a Jewish burial ground without dedicated halachic oversight. Work involving historic Jewish cemeteries requires extraordinary precautions to prevent any disturbance of graves. Organizations specializing in cemetery preservation generally insist that such projects be conducted under experienced halachic supervision. The Brzesko cemetery is the resting place of numerous Rabbanim and tzaddikim, including Rav Aryeh Leibush Lipschitz zt”l, the Aryeh D’Bei Ila’i; Rav Meshulam Zalman Yonasan ben Rav Aryeh Leib zt”l; Rav Pinchas Templer of Dembitz-Briegel; Rav Pinchas Templer ben Rav Mattisyahu, known as Reb Pinchas’l Dembitzer and Reb Pinchas’l Briegeler; Rav Menashe ben Rav Menachem or Nachum Tzvi zt”l; and Rav Tuvia ben Rav Meshulam Zalman zt”l. Meir Bulka, chairman of J-nerations, sharply condemned what occurred. “This is not the first time we have seen the Jewish community of Krakow act contrary to the way of halacha,” Bulka said. “Unfortunately, for years, foreign interests have been driving the conduct of this community, whose Jewish past is questionable, and no one speaks up. The Jewish people must cry out through every possible means and stand firm to prevent them from operating without halachic supervision and through methods involving the theft of Jewish money, from people whose only desire is to visit the graves of their ancestors and daven at the graves of tzaddikim.” The incident has sparked outrage among activists involved in protecting Jewish cemeteries in Poland, who are demanding that any further work at the site be halted unless proper halachic supervision is put in place. (YWN World Headquarters – NYC) 3 Responses A Chillul H”M. The preservation of a grave is not just about the earth and stone that mark a resting place. It is about the memory held within that earth, the link between generations. To disrupt that is to sever a chain, to diminish the very idea of continuity. The remains scattered are not merely bones; they are pieces of a story, a lineage. The desecration of a Jewish cemetery, especially one holding the remains of Rabbanim and tzaddikim, is a profound wound. The scattering of human remains and damage to graves without halachic supervision is unacceptable. Protecting these sacred spaces requires unwavering vigilance and respect for Jewish law. We must ensure that such incidents are never repeated and that all work on Jewish burial sites is conducted with the utmost care and proper oversight. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Police patrol the perimeter of RAF Fairford as a US bomber lands. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA View image in fullscreen Police patrol the perimeter of RAF Fairford as a US bomber lands. Photograph: Ben Birchall/PA UK news UK-Iran national arrested over alleged bomb plot at RAF Fairford released on bail The 25-year-old was the sixth man detained as counter-terrorism police investigate ‘possible foreign state involvement’ PA Media Sat 3 Oct 2026 09.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A sixth man who was arrested in connection with a suspected terrorist plot at RAF Fairford has been released on bail. The 25-year-old, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts under section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. He was detained on Thursday in the borough of Westminster, London, where searches of two properties have now concluded. The investigation into the incident is still under way, counter-terrorism police said. Last weekend, five British nationals, all in their mid-20s, were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and terrorism and then bailed. The arrests were made after three suspicious vans were spotted near the military site in Gloucestershire. View image in fullscreen Five men were arrested last weekend after police were alerted to suspicious vans near RAF Fairford. Photograph: BBC Vicki Evans, the senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, previously said the investigation was “hugely complex”, adding that specialist teams were “interrogating multiple lines of inquiry”. She said: “As we’ve made clear, we’re looking at all possible angles – including possible foreign state involvement.” The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has said there were “strong indications” Iran played a part in the incident near the Gloucestershire military base. RAF Fairford has been used in recent months by US bombers after former prime minister Keir Starmer granted Washington permission to use British bases for “defensive” strikes against Tehran. View image in fullscreen A B‑1B Lancer bomber departs RAF Fairford airbase after police declared a major incident at the base last weekend. Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Reuters Counter-terrorism police have said a quantity of petrol, but no explosive devices, was found in the vans that had sparked the security alert near the airbase. On Thursday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, claimed Israel handed Britain intelligence about the suspected terror plot. Netanyahu said his country warned UK authorities about the “Iranian-sponsored attack” shortly before Britain’s announcement of a ban on trade with illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank. https://en.interfax.com.ua/news/general/.text: Slovak Prosecutor General Maroš Žilinka has decided to reopen the case concerning the transfer of military equipment to Ukraine by the country’s previous government in 2023. "After reviewing the case, I have concluded that the decision to close it was premature," Žilinka wrote on social media. He stated that the investigation must be resumed and that the relevant directive has been issued to the prosecutor in the city of Trenčín. The case concerns the transfer to Ukraine of 13 MiG-29 fighter jets and Kub (SA-6 Gainful) surface-to-air missile systems that had been in service with the Slovak Armed Forces. In February 2026, Bratislava prosecutor Rastislav Remeta, upon concluding a preliminary investigation, stated that the transferred fighter jets and air defense systems were obsolete and that their transfer to Ukraine did not constitute a criminal offense.
